claims.text: Premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed primarily by temperature-induced surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Atomic size mismatch and surface-energy imbalances drive the proposed surface segregation.
Gradual heating produces a surface layer enriched in lower-melting-point elements.
Reduced coordination of surface atoms and differences in elemental surface energies promote atomic diffusion and segregation during heating.
The segregated surface forms a chemically distinct phase with a melting point below that of the bulk material.
The depressed melting point of the segregated surface phase causes local surface premelting before the particle bulk melts.
Surface disorder and partial liquefaction begin below the reported bulk melting point.
Particles in which surface segregation is inhibited should premelt at a higher temperature than particles with unaltered surfaces.
Nanoparticles with minimal surface segregation should melt more uniformly across their structure.
Protective coatings or rapid quenching can inhibit surface segregation in the proposed comparison.
The proposed mechanism should apply to high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with significant atomic-size disparities and configurational entropy.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to particles smaller than approximately 3 nm.
Other interfacial phenomena can dominate thermal behavior outside the proposed range.
Variation in synthesis conditions can alter the degree of segregation and the magnitude of premelting-temperature depression.
